title: Static Stretching and Human Movement: Integrating Tissue Mechanics, Neuromechanical Responses, and Functional Performance
content: Static stretching is widely used in sports medicine, rehabilitation, and exercise science to improve joint range of motion (ROM) and flexibility. However, its effects on human movement remain incompletely understood because biomechanical out-comes—including ROM, passive mechanical properties, force production, power output, stretch–shortening cycle function, jumping performance, landing biomechanics, and postural stability—have often been examined separately. Consequently, the relation-ships among tissue-level responses, neuromechanical responses, and task-specific func-tional outcomes remain incompletely integrated. This integrative review synthesizes current evidence across these biomechanical domains and proposes a framework for interpreting their relationships without assuming a fixed causal or sequential pathway. Current evidence indicates that static stretching consistently increases ROM, whereas changes in passive mechanical properties are more tissue- and protocol-dependent. Acute static stretching may transiently reduce maximal force and power, particularly following longer stretching durations, whereas repeated stretching generally produces neutral or modestly beneficial effects on strength-related outcomes. Effects on power and stretch–shortening cycle function, jumping performance, landing biomechanics, and postural stability are more heterogeneous and vary according to stretching exposure, participant characteristics, task demands, and testing conditions. Importantly, responses observed within one biomechanical domain do not necessarily correspond proportion-ally to changes in another, indicating that functional transfer may be complete, partial, or absent. The proposed integrative biomechanical framework therefore conceptualizes static stretching as a mechanical stimulus associated with interacting tissue-level, neu-romechanical, and task-specific functional responses. Neuromuscular and sensorimotor regulation operates across these domains, while contextual and methodological factors may moderate their functional expression. Overall, static stretching should be under-stood not solely as an intervention for increasing flexibility but as a biomechanical stimulus whose effects on human movement depend on the interaction of mechanical, neural, task-specific, and contextual factors. This perspective provides a framework for interpreting heterogeneous findings while avoiding assumptions of causal or sequential functional transfer across biomechanical domains.
